claims.text: Traditional EAM references cannot adequately represent the multiplicity of atomic configurations in the ab initio liquid state of multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
An actively learned MLIP can better capture the multiplicity of atomic configurations in the ab initio liquid than a traditional EAM reference.
Using an MLIP as the thermodynamic-integration reference will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
Using an MLIP as the reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
The proposed intervention applies to multicomponent, chemically disordered high-entropy alloys, including refractory equimolar alloys with at least five principal elements.
The proposed temperature range is near melting, exemplified by temperatures at or above approximately 0.8 times the melting temperature.
The MLIP should be trained on a diverse set of ab initio configurations representing both disordered liquid and solid phases.
Entropy plays a dominant role near the melting temperature in the systems under consideration.
Learning many-body interactions and configurational variability from ab initio data causes the MLIP reference to overlap more closely with the target ab initio phase space.
Training on representative atomic configurations allows an MLIP reference to follow a smoother thermodynamic-integration path.
A smoother MLIP-based integration path has fewer energetic discontinuities between the reference and target states.
The MLIP reference is expected to reduce integration-path mismatch by approximately 30–50% or more relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
MLIP-based free-energy estimates are expected to deviate from direct ab initio AIMD benchmarks by only a few meV per atom.
Existing TOR-TILD calculations using EAM references exhibit marked phase-space gaps in the liquid state.
The MLIP approach may be less reliable in alloys with strong local chemical ordering.
The MLIP approach may be less reliable when high-quality MLIP training data are sparse.
The quantitative reduction in path mismatch depends on alloy chemistry, sampled configurations, and training-dataset quality.

Failure to achieve both free-energy agreement within ±5 meV/atom of the AIMD benchmark and at least approximately 30% statistically significant mismatch reduction relative to EAM would falsify the hypothesis.
